title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: Your makerspace assistant's code always runs three steps in this order: look up the manual page, call the model to draft an answer, then call the model to check the draft. Who decides that order of steps?

options.text: The model, which chooses each next step as it works on the question
The student, through the way the question is worded to the assistant
The program's code, which the developers wrote before any question arrived
The tool descriptions, which tell the model what order to follow here

items.stem: Which part of the makerspace assistant is the best candidate for a fixed workflow rather than an agent?

options.text: Booking a machine once the student has confirmed the machine, date and time
Working out why a student's laser cuts keep coming out burnt and uneven
Answering an unclear question such as "my print failed, what do I do?"
Planning a project that needs several machines and many different manuals

items.stem: In one sentence, what is the difference between a workflow and an agent, in terms of who controls the sequence of steps?

Every manual question in your assistant needs the same steps: search the manuals, then write an answer from the pages found. Your sponsor gave you a small model budget. Why is a fixed workflow often the better choice here?

options.text: A workflow has no model in it, so no model usage fees are charged
Only a workflow is able to call a search tool over the manual pages
A workflow gives better answers than an agent on every kind of task
The number of model calls is known in advance, so cost is predictable

items.stem: A fixed workflow for a manual question always makes 2 model calls. An agent doing the same job makes 5 model calls on average. Over 200 questions, how many more model calls does the agent make than the workflow? Assume the question count is the only difference.
In one sentence, what must be true about a task for an agent to be a better choice than a fixed workflow?
